item.title: HFCL, Sterlite Tech shares rally 5% each as Nvidia’s strong earnings eclipse AI worries
item.description: HFCL and Sterlite Technologies shares rally 5% each as Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings and revenue outlook revive optimism around AI infrastructure spending. The gains follow a decline of more than 10% in both stocks over two sessions. Investors are also assessing concerns around US data centre expansion and AI sector valuations.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Shares of optical fibre manufacturers HFCL and Sterlite Tech, whose products are extensively used in AI infrastructure, rallied 5% each on Wednesday after AI bellwether Nvidia reported third-quarter earnings and revenue above Wall Street expectations and issued a fourth-quarter revenue forecast that exceeded analyst estimates. Nvidia shares gained over 5% in after-hours trading.The gains also came after shares of the two companies fell more than 10% over two days, suggesting value buying at lower levels. The uptick also came despite concerns that the Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections could bring tighter restrictions on data centre expansion, potentially slowing the development of the country's AI infrastructure.Nvidia's strong earnings are positive for HFCL and Sterlite Tech because they reinforce expectations of sustained AI infrastructure spending globally. This benefits HFCL and Sterlite Tech because AI data centres require extensive optical fibre networks for high-speed, low-latency data transmission and connectivity between servers and facilities.Nvidia's results came as investors continued to assess the company's leadership transition following the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia said it would not entertain questions about Huang's resignation and had no plans to reinstate him.Interim CEO Colette Kress told investors that the company expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal 2028.For the fourth quarter, Nvidia projected revenue of $126 billion to $134 billion, comfortably ahead of the average analyst estimate of just over $125 billion, according to LSEG data. The company clarified that its forecast did not factor in any data centre chip sales to China.“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” Kress said.Sensex, Nifty today; Catch all the LIVE stock market updates here Where is AI headed?The data centre slowdown due to the political shift is going to be real, and the earnings estimates behind the valuations that were the cornerstone of bullish arguments are no longer valid, according to Michael O’Rourke at JonesTrading.“Investors have no idea where those estimates will reset,” he said. “As a result, they are de-risking until clarity returns, which won’t be for some time.”Where this differs from a regular sell-off is that we are not seeing recoveries after significant losses, such as Intel Corp. falling further this week even after plunging almost 30% on Friday, according to Jakub Rochlitz at eToro. There’s also increasing cross-sector correlation and a rise in volatility, meaning that the rout is spreading across the market.“The all-or-nothing mentality is surprising to us, because we believe the real truth is more nuanced,” said Chris Zaccarelli at Northlight Asset Management. “We do agree that sentiment has shifted and building data centres will become more difficult, but if there is a productive business case for building them, then they will get built.”The next major indicator of investor appetite for the AI sector will come from Anthropic, which is preparing to set the price of its shares later on Wednesday ahead of its market debut. The listing could value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion. Anthropic has indicated that it is targeting an IPO price at the upper end of its range or potentially above it, Bloomberg News reported.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. item.title: TCS, Infosys, other IT stocks fall up to 3% as Nvidia earnings beat eases AI fears; South Korea’s Kospi rises over 3%
item.description: Shares of major IT conglomerates, including TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, experienced a decline following Nvidia's impressive earnings announcement. The company revealed a promising revenue forecast for the next fiscal year, signaling stability amid management transitions. This shift raised questions about the durability of AI investments as Nvidia's market value was reevaluated.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Shares of IT companies such as TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech, Tech Mahindra, and Wipro declined up to 3% on Wednesday as AI major Nvidia reported third-quarter earnings and revenue above Wall Street expectations and issued a fourth-quarter revenue forecast that exceeded analyst estimates.In today's session, TCS shares dipped 2.5% to Rs 2,382, while Infosys was down almost a per cent to Rs 1,113. Wipro also slipped over a per cent, while HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra fell up to 1%.The results came as investors continued to assess the company's leadership transition following the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia said it would not entertain questions about Huang's resignation and had no plans to reinstate him.Interim CEO Colette Kress told investors that the company expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal 2028.For the fourth quarter, Nvidia projected revenue of $126 billion to $134 billion, comfortably ahead of the average analyst estimate of just over $125 billion, according to LSEG data. The company clarified that its forecast did not factor in any data centre chip sales to China.“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” Kress said.Nvidia shares gained 1% in after-hours trading as earnings came in after the closing bell. The stock has declined in 12 of the past 15 sessions and is down 25% this month.Nvidia's estimated forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio has fallen to approximately 11.3 times, its lowest level since 2011, putting the valuation of the world's leading AI chipmaker under scrutiny as investors reassess the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment cycle.The multiple is also significantly below Nvidia's forward P/E interquartile range of 30-44 times over the past decade, reflecting growing concerns around AI infrastructure financing, leadership uncertainty and the durability of future earnings, according to Binance Research.Asian AI stocks advanceAsian technology stocks moved higher, with MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rising 0.9%. South Korea's KOSPI led the gains, climbing as much as 3.3%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 0.6%. US S&P 500 e-mini futures were also up 0.5%.The next major indicator of investor appetite for the AI sector will come from Anthropic, which is preparing to set the price of its shares later on Wednesday ahead of its market debut. The listing could value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion. Anthropic has indicated that it is targeting an IPO price at the upper end of its range or potentially above it, Bloomberg News reported.Where is AI headed?The data centre slowdown due to the political shift is going to be real, and the earnings estimates behind the valuations that were the cornerstone of bullish arguments are no longer valid, according to Michael O’Rourke at JonesTrading.“Investors have no idea where those estimates will reset,” he said. “As a result, they are de-risking until clarity returns, which won’t be for some time.”Michael Burry, who made his name shorting the US housing market, said he sold 25% of his put positions in the $58 billion VanEck Semiconductor ETF amid a deepening rout in US technology stocks. “The SMH put positions even after the sale, however, have become very large positions,” he wrote.Where this differs from a regular sell-off is that we are not seeing recoveries after significant losses, such as Intel Corp. falling further this week even after plunging almost 30% on Friday, according to Jakub Rochlitz at eToro. There’s also increasing cross-sector correlation and a rise in volatility, meaning that the rout is spreading across the market.“The all-or-nothing mentality is surprising to us, because we believe the real truth is more nuanced,” said Chris Zaccarelli at Northlight Asset Management. “We do agree that sentiment has shifted and building data centres will become more difficult, but if there is a productive business case for building them, then they will get built.”Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser.
